description:
A new top-level workspace crate `gf2-algebra` that reproduces and beats arxiv 2407.20205v2 (Scheinerman, fast permanents over $\mathbb{F}_3$ via $\mathbb{F}_2$ arithmetic) by $\ge 50\times$ single-thread, plus parallel scaling and HIP/ROCm GPU, with Lean4 verification. ## Background The reference paper introduces a "bipedal" map encoding $\mathbb{F}_3^n$ as a pair of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ vectors and implements add/sub/mul/div in 1–6 bitwise ops each. Combined with Ryser's permanent formula in Gray-code subset order, the inner loop becomes effectively $O(2^n)$ primitive `u64` operations for $n \le 64$. The paper reports an $86.9\times$ speedup over a naive Ryser implementation in Julia, single-thread, on a 4.20 GHz desktop. The paper does not exploit SIMD, multicore, or GPU — that is our headroom. This epic adds the new crate `gf2-algebra` and: 1. Reproduces the paper's `permanent_mod3` algorithm in Rust as an in-tree baseline. 2. Beats it by $\ge 50\times$ single-thread via AVX2 (and AVX-512 where available) bipedal SIMD kernels in `gf2-kernels-simd`. 3. Adds rayon parallel scaling and HIP/ROCm GPU kernels in `gf2-kernels-hip`. 4. Generalises to $\mathbb{F}_5$ and $\mathbb{F}_7$ via best-effort encoding research (`type:simulation` children). 5. Mechanically verifies (Lean4 via Charon/Aeneas) the bipedal $\mathbb{F}_3$ arithmetic and Ryser's formula on the project's `FiniteField` trait, scoped to the bounded $n \le 63$ single-`u64` regime. 6. Produces a publication-grade benchmark artefact (criterion + plots + reproducible scripts). The full design — wave plan ($W_0 \ldots W_7$, $\sim 48$ children), `PackedField` trait surface, encoding plans, hardware envelope (dev host: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X, AVX2 only — AVX-512 paths are `[aspirational]`), and risk register — is in the linked design doc. ## Success Criteria - [ ] [hard] A new workspace crate `gf2-algebra` exists, builds clean under `cargo nextest run --workspace --all-features --release --profile ci`, and is registered in the workspace `Cargo.toml`. - [ ] [hard] `gf2-algebra::permanent::permanent_bipedal3` produces values bit-identical to the generic `permanent_ryser` over `Fp<3>` on 1000 random matrices for every $n \in \{1, \ldots, 16\}$ and on 100 random matrices for $n \in \{20, 24, 28, 32\}$. - [ ] [hard] `gf2-algebra::permanent::permanent_bipedal3` (single-thread, AVX2 path) runs $n=36$ random $\{-1, 0, 1\}$ matrices $\ge 50\times$ faster than the in-tree `permanent_mod3_reference` (faithful Rust port of paper Julia) on the same machine. - [ ] [aspirational] Same comparison vs the paper's published Julia number on a documented Zen 4/5 reference host: $\ge 50\times$ speedup at $n=36$. - [ ] [hard for $n \ge 28$] `permanent_bipedal3` parallel scaling factor is $\ge 0.85\times$ per physical core up to the host's physical core count. - [ ] [hard] $\mathbb{F}_5$ and $\mathbb{F}_7$ packed permanents return values matching `permanent_ryser` over the corresponding `Fp

` on 1000 random matrices for $n \in \{1, \ldots, 14\}$. - [ ] [hard] Lean4 proof of bipedal $\mathbb{F}_3$ correctness vs `Fp<3>` builds with `lake build` and contains no `sorry`. - [ ] [hard] Lean4 proof of Ryser's formula on `FiniteField` (bounded $n \le 63$) builds with `lake build` and contains no `sorry`. - [ ] [hard] A reproducible benchmark artefact lives in `dev/benchmarks/gf2_algebra_permanent/`, with criterion JSONs, hardware fingerprint, seed pins, and `scripts/permanent-repro.sh` runs end-to-end. - [ ] [aspirational] GPU permanent crossover at $n \ge 40$ for $\mathbb{F}_3$ on gfx1030. - [ ] [hard] Root `CLAUDE.md` and `ROADMAP.md` are updated to reference `gf2-algebra`. - [ ] [hard] `cargo run -p gf2-algebra --example permanent_demo --release` produces the headline benchmark numbers within $\pm 5\%$. ## Notes Non-goals: - General-purpose char-3 linear algebra (det, rank, char-poly, Smith normal form) — natural follow-up, out of scope here. - Permanents over $\mathbb{F}_2$ ($\operatorname{perm} = \det$; already trivial via existing rank/RREF code). - Primes $p \ge 11$. - Proof of unbounded-$n$ Ryser (requires formalising arbitrary-arity sums; would explode V2 scope). - Reproducing the paper's $n=50$ / 832 CPU-hour 128-core run literally — a smaller analogous run will demonstrate the speedup factor. ## Amendment 2026-05-10 (user-approved — trim large-n cross-check) Success criterion 2 originally required `permanent_bipedal3` cross-checks at `n ∈ {20, 24, 28, 32}` × 100 matrices each against the generic `permanent_ryser`. Per the empirical measurement summarised in T9 (`b0857ae9`)'s `## Amendment 2026-05-10` block, the n=28 and n=32 cases are computationally infeasible at 100 matrices (≥ 36 hr and ~8 days respectively against either oracle). **Amended criterion 2 (large-n):** `permanent_bipedal3` produces values bit-identical to `permanent_ryser>` on 1000 random matrices for every `n ∈ {1, ..., 16}` (as before) and on 100 random matrices for `n ∈ {20, 24}` only. The dropped sizes (`n ∈ {28, 32}`) are spot-checked at smaller matrix counts via the SIMD batch path (T12) and the multi-word streaming path (T14) once those land in W3. The 50× perf criterion (success criterion 3) is unchanged: `permanent_bipedal3` at n=36 still must beat `permanent_mod3_reference` by ≥ 50×. Performance measurement is `Criterion`-driven, with seed pinning, not full cross-check; the 50× target is `criterion::black_box` median over a small matrix set, not 100-matrix bit-identical cross-validation. Approved by user 2026-05-10 (epic ae82bd73 session 3, AskUserQuestion option A). ## Amendment 2026-05-11 (user-approved, Option A — oracle for large-n cross-check) Following the 2026-05-10 trim of criterion 2's $n$ range to $\{20, 24\}$, T9's rework-cycle-1 code review surfaced that `permanent_ryser>` at $n = 24$ takes ~80 s/matrix on the dev host (AMD Ryzen 9 5900X), which exceeds the slow-tier 120 s/test budget for 100 matrices. **Amended criterion 2 (oracle):** For $n \in \{1, \ldots, 16\}$ the oracle remains `permanent_ryser>`. For $n \in \{20, 24\}$ the cross-check may use `permanent_mod3_reference` (paper-faithful Julia port, T8 `632d92ad`) as the oracle, on the strength of T8's own bit-identical cross-check vs `permanent_ryser>` at $n \le 12$ for 12000 matrices (T8 criterion). Transitivity: T8 ↔ T7 at small $n$ + T9 ↔ T8 at $n \in \{20, 24\}$ implies T9 ↔ T7 at $n \in \{20, 24\}$. `permanent_mod3_reference` is roughly 10× faster than `permanent_ryser>` (no trait-call overhead per Gray step), so 100 matrices at $n = 24$ runs in ~800 s — feasible split across per-$n$ `#[ignore = "sim: ..."]` tests under nightly slow-tier. Approved by user 2026-05-11 (epic ae82bd73 session 4, AskUserQuestion option A on T9 oracle).
